Ok now if I want to publish taxkit as packages, how can we do that.
I’ll check the package setup and current npm publishing requirements, then outline what we’d need to change and how to publish from your Mac.

We can publish TaxKit to **npm from your Mac**, keeping GitHub CI out of the process.

I’d start with the existing **ten-package `2.0.0` release group**, with `@taxkit/sdk` as the main package people install. The website, infrastructure and other internal packages can stay private.

The process would be:

1. **Confirm the npm account and name.** We need publishing access to the `@taxkit` namespace. That ownership hasn’t been verified yet.
2. **Prepare the selected packages.** Remove `private: true` only from those packages, confirm their licence and repository details, and check that the downloadable packages contain built JavaScript and TypeScript types.
3. **Test the actual package files.** Run the local release checks, inspect the packed files, and install them into a fresh project. Dependencies must contain ordinary version numbers rather than repository-only `workspace:` or `catalog:` references.
4. **Publish locally, dependencies first.** Sign in to npm and complete its two-factor authentication prompts. Public scoped packages use `--access public`. [npm publishing guide](https://docs.npmjs.com/creating-and-publishing-scoped-public-packages/)
5. **Verify the published result.** Install from npm into another fresh project, run calculations, and confirm every published version and dependency.

Afterward, users could install it with:

```sh
npm install @taxkit/sdk
```

One trade-off: local publishing works, but npm’s build-provenance badge currently requires a supported hosted CI service. [npm provenance requirements](https://docs.npmjs.com/generating-provenance-statements/)

The versions and local package checks are already in place. The remaining work is **npm ownership, publication settings and verifying a real registry installation**.

| Package | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `@taxkit/sdk` | Main library people install to run calculations |
| `@taxkit/core` | Calculation engine and shared money, date and rule types |
| `@taxkit/calculators` | Ready-to-use calculator operations |
| `@taxkit/rules-au-income-tax` | Australian annual income tax and Medicare rules |
| `@taxkit/rules-au-pay` | PAYG withholding and take-home pay rules |

| `@taxkit/content` | Documentation page data, navigation and search |
| `@taxkit/testing` | Helpers for testing calculations |
| `@taxkit/tsconfig` | Shared TypeScript compiler settings |

The website, deployment infrastructure and other internal packages would stay private.

Your organisation supports names such as `@taxkit/sdk`. The bare name `taxkit` would be a separate package. [npm scope explanation](https://docs.npmjs.com/about-scopes/)
Should we adopt the approach that Effect has taken in v4 where there's one package to install?
I’ll check Effect v4’s package structure and compare it with TaxKit’s dependencies, then recommend what would make installation simplest.

**Yes — one main public package is a better starting point for TaxKit. I’d revise my earlier ten-package recommendation.**

Effect v4 brought many modules into `effect`, while keeping some platform integrations separate. That’s the useful pattern to follow. [Effect’s explanation](https://effect.website/blog/releases/effect/40)

Using our existing scoped name, the proposed shape would be:

```sh
npm install @taxkit/sdk
```

| Import | What it provides |
|---|---|
| `@taxkit/sdk` | Simple calculation functions |
| `@taxkit/sdk/au` | Australian calculators and rules |
| `@taxkit/sdk/effect` | Effect-native operations |
| `@taxkit/sdk/core` | Engine and lower-level building blocks |
| `@taxkit/sdk/http` | HTTP API contracts and helpers |

Those are different entry points **inside the same installed package**.

The existing SDK already offers one install command, but npm would currently need to fetch several separate TaxKit packages. Consolidating publication would give us one public version, one changelog and fewer compatibility problems.

We can keep the source organised into clear modules internally. The published package would contain their built code, with no dependencies on unpublished `@taxkit/*` packages. Effect would remain an external dependency.

Website deployment, infrastructure, repository TypeScript settings and internal testing tools should stay outside the main package. We’d also check that browser imports don’t load server code.

The trade-off is releasing the engine and tax rules together—which our current versioning already does. **I’d make this change before the first npm publication.**
Yes, implement the single-package approach with those entry points. Run the checks locally, merge to main and clean up. Keep GitHub CI off and don't publish to npm yet.

I’ll build one installable package with those five entry points, keep it private, and test it in a fresh project. Then I’ll run the local checks, merge to `main` and clean up, with GitHub CI skipped as requested.
